newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin tells still unknown new govt to fix crisis.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin tells still unknown new govt to fix crisis.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin is to unveil a new government early this week which will be charged with undertaking further economic reforms and, most pressingly, averting Russia's deepening social crisis.

Labour unions, backed by the communist-led parliament, plan a day of protest on March 27. Millions of workers have not been paid for months. Coalminers have already staged strikes. Some opposition leaders warn Yeltsin could face Albanian-style anarchy and be unable to control unrest due to low morale in the army.

March 27 may have been on Yeltsin's mind on Saturday when, with the cabinet still in limbo, he ordered the goverment to sort out financial problems affecting rations for the troops and pay its debts to the coal industry to spare the miners hardship.
"Take steps urgently," Yeltsin told the cabinet.
The 66-year-old leader goes to Helsinki on Wednesday for a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton that will be dominated by talks on lowering Moscow's objections to NATO expansion.
Any weakness on Yeltsin's part could only fuel discontent at home. He told a Finnish newspaper on Sunday that Russia insisted on a binding treaty barring western forces from eastern Europe.

The liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta noted that Defence Minister Igor Rodionov met commanders on Friday to discuss poor morale among officers. The paper said the ministry even considered that civil unrest could turn the army against Moscow's rulers.

"The possibility of a social explosion among the troops threatens to repeat an 'Albanian scenario' in which the army does not counter unrest and ex-officers lead the mutineers' attacks on the central authorities," it said.
Defence analysts discount the chances of organised revolt in the army -- it is hardly in a fit state to organise anything. But few rule out the possibility of localised incidents.
General Alexander Lebed, Yeltsin's former security chief, said on Friday that March 27 may be a catalyst that could sweep the president from power and put Lebed himself in the Kremlin.
Major political upheaval appears unlikely, especially as the Helsinki talks should indicate Yeltsin has recovered well enough from heart surgery and pneumonia to see out his term to 2000.
But in a state of the nation address this month, the president acknowledged that "people's patience is running out".

A VTsIOM poll last week showed 79 percent of Russians disapproved of his policies. Anatoly Chubais, the Kremlin aide Yeltsin has made first deputy prime minister and charged with reviving the economy, had an 85-percent disapproval rating.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, 58, said on Saturday the restructuring of the government was nearly ready. He promised new faces, a weeding out of Soviet-style industrial ministries and a determined approach to push through unpopular decisions.
Chubais, 41, would be in overall charge of the economy.
"We cannot drag out the process of reform," Chernomyrdin told ORT television. "We cannot drag out people's suffering."

The Kremlin says Yeltsin will announce the changes on Monday or Tuesday. Chernomyrdin said negotiations on the new team had been hard. Analysts have speculated Chubais may have faced opposition from industrial monopolies, who see Chernomyrdin, a former gas industry chief, as a guarantor of their interests.
Liberal opposition leader Grigory Yavlinsky said at the weekend: "As long as Chernomyrdin heads the government...any fight against the natural monopolies is just show."
Yeltsin recently denounced the corrupt embrace of government and business, which he said was strangling genuine free markets.
Yet one of his top aides, Georgy Satarov, was quoted saying this weekend that graft had oiled the transition to capitalism.
The Kremlin was also force to moved at the weekend to stem talk of scandal over the appointment of Yeltsin's son-in-law, Valery Okulov, to head state-controlled airline Aeroflot.
Spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky was quoted by Ekho Moskvy radio saying Yeltsin did nothing to help his daughter's husband get the job.
